newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FEATURE-Australian electricity heads into high-volt trade.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Australian electricity heads into high-volt trade.

text.p: Progressive deregulation of Australia's A$12 billion-a-year power industry has turned electricity into a highly-charged traded commodity.

Already about half of the electricity generated in the main power-producing states of New South Wales (NSW) and Victoria is being traded in the form of contracts between electricity customers and generators, following the establishment of published pool prices in the past two years.
Hour-to-hour volatility in electricity prices has helped boost interest in the market.

Under deregulation plans, the full annual electricity output of Australia's two main states of about 90,000 gigawatt (GW) hours, or more than half Australia's total production of about 160,000 GW hours, will be traded by 2000.
"A GREAT BIG PIE"

Electricity has become one of the most commercially sensitive products in Australia as the deregulation process unfolds. State-owned power groups, once comparatively insulated from market pressures, have quickly become a focus of the commercial world.
"There's lots of sticky fingers in a great big pie. And the merchant bankers seem to be making the money," said one executive in a major electricity group, who asked not to be named.

Australia's eastern-state electricity markets have been transformed into a mosaic of declining numbers of vested contracts between generators and retailers and a rising proportion of physically-traded electricity.
Derivative products such as swaps and options already cover a large part of the physical market.
But the sector has been developing so quickly that industry executives have been hard-pressed to keep pace.
Some industry executives said about half of NSW electricity was already being freely traded, one way or another.

Industry estimates value the NSW traded wholesale electricity market at about A$23 million (US$17.46 million) a week, or often around A$5 million a day. Financial intermediaries said the derivatives market also often turns over this amount or more.
Electricity trading is conceptually simple.

Retailers and generators agree on deals in advance of contract delivery because of significant hour-to-hour volatility in spot electricity prices. The price agreement may then be traded or form the basis of swaps and options arranged by intermediaries.
Macquarie Bank and others have already been active in this.
But the practice is far more complicated than the theory, as the Sydney Futures Exchange (SFE) has found as it investigates listing electricity futures in August or September.
FLAT OR SCULPTED?
The SFE has been grappling with what it calls "contract specification" as the key to a potentially lucrative market in electricity futures.
A spokesman for the SFE told Reuters that issues such as whether short-dated or long-dated contracts would be listed were under examination. Long-dated contracts will most likely be listed first.
Contracts were likely to be set on a monthly basis 12 months ahead and based on a monthly average of prices from the NSW government-owned transmission operator Transgrid.
Contract size will be crucial in gearing market liquidity and turnover -- a 500 megawatt contract is under consideration -- as is whether prices will be flat or sculpted.

Flat prices have the advantage of simplicity, sculpted prices, which reflect physical market volatility from hour to hour, the advantage of greater realism. The SFE was also pondering listing NSW or Victorian futures, or both.
Randell Heyman, director of Macquarie Bank's treasury and commodities group, said his group supported the SFE's endeavours and anything which increased liquidity in markets.
BIG DOLLARS IN POWER
"The market is big, a lot of dollars are at risk and futures should find a place," another industry executive said.
But the unanswered question for everybody involved is the likely market size.
The approximately A$5 million a day turnover of physical electricity in NSW is one rough guide. But then, the A$5 million turnover figure is itself not accepted by all.

Futures would not initially capture all of the physical market, but after a year or so might achieve multiples of the physical market, as had occurred with international oil, an industry source said. The market could be big, sources said.
Electricity futures as the latest likely development in a fast-moving electricity market, were seen to be aided by big privatisation moves in the NSW and Victorian electricity industries.
"Privatised organisations have balance sheets on the line," one source said. Risk management would become more critical as organisations become less insulated from the market.
NSW Treasurer Michael Egan has put forward a A$22 billion privatisation proposal for the state's electricity industry, primarily three generation companies.

NSW already faces fierce competition from aggressive private players after Victoria's electricity privatisations, which have so far raised about A$18 billion. Major Victorian sales have been the Loy Yang, Yallourn and Hazelwood power stations, mainly to United States and other foreign interests.

Major developments now occur almost week-by-week, with a NSW wholesale electricity market beginning in March this year and a retail market being opened to "full contestability" by private competition by July 1999.
The first stage of a national electricity market started last month, allowing interstate power trading between NSW and Victoria for the first time.
